datasets.description_excerpt:
The dataset comprises of images from an industrial agrochemical crystallization process with needle-like shape morphology. Data is collected from three batches of the active ingredient with different crystal size distributions. 

The particles were collected in-situ using an EasyViewer 100 probe where pre-weighed solids were slurried with a known amount of mother liquor to create a known solid loading composition. Starting from lowest solid concentration, images were collected for increasing solid loading concentrations by adding more solid material. The Morphologi G3 was used for off-line crystal size measurement (ground-truth).

datasets.description_excerpt:
The dataset comprises of images obtained during a cephalexin monohydrate crystallization process. This process involved creating a slurry of cephalexin monohydrate crystals through a seeded batch crystallization technique. In-situ images were taken from the slurry using a Mettler-Toledo EasyViewer-100 probe. Initially, these images featured a pure cephalexin monohydrate slurry without any byproduct crystals. Subsequently, impurity phenylglycine crystals were incrementally introduced into the slurry. In-situ images were captured once again. 

The image dataset is categorized into two parts: Raw and Cropped images, which correspond to different treatments of the original PVM image. Raw images represent the unprocessed images acquired by the probe. Cropped images, on the other hand, showcase instances of either cephalexin or phenylglycine crystals. Both the raw and cropped image folders are further subdivided into two sub-folders: one for cephalexin crystals (the target product) and another for phenylglycine crystals (the byproduct). A process monitoring goal can be detecting the presence of impurity in the system.

|Name|	Crystallization impurity detection|
| --- | --- |
|Problem type|	Image classification, anomaly detection|
|Number of images|	+400 raw images, +6000 cropped images|
|Microscopy type|	In-situ|
|Image format|	png|
|PAT hardware|	EasyViewer-100||

datasets.description_excerpt:
The dataset comprises images from two different particle systems namely a) Vansil ® WG Wollastonite particles and b) L-Glutamic acid particles. The images were captured in situ using two different EasyViewer probes (EasyViewer 100 and EasyViewer 400) where pre-weighed solids were suspended in solvent to create a known solid loading composition. Along with the images, in-line Chord Length Distribution (CLD) data was also measured with the ParticleTrack G400 probe. The developed image analysis algorithm can be validated using either the CLD data collected in situ or with the manufacturer's size data provided for the Wollastonite dataset. 


# System A: Vansil ® WG Wollastonite 
Wollastonite, a natural calcium silicate mineral known for its elevated brightness, serves as an effective functional filler and reinforcement in various materials such as thermoplastics, thermosets, engineering alloys, and elastomers. The distinctive needle-like shape and high aspect ratio of VANSIL wollastonite particles contribute to enhanced mechanical strength and stiffness, while simultaneously improving surface quality, toughness, and durability. To produce VANSIL WG, the ore containing wollastonite is milled in such a way that the fine, needle-like particles are preserved and recovered.  It is used as a sample system as it is easy to prepare, stable, and optically similar to many particles found in small molecule crystallizations. 

## Properties
1.	Average Aspect Ratio: 15:1
2.	Average Needle Length: 90um
3.	200 mesh retention, %: 15-20%
4.	325 mesh retention, %: 30-35%
5.	Density: 2.9 g/cm^3

datasets.description_excerpt:
*In-situ* images of several sizes of polystyrene standard microspheres. These images are a good resources for validating and comparing object detection methods. 

# Data Collection
Samples of polystyrene microspheres of nominal diameters 200um, 300um, 400um, and 500um were obtained from Fisher Scientific, and 150um from Sigma-Aldrich. These samples were suspended in deionised water at several weight concentrations (2wt%, 2.5wt%, 3.3wt%, 5wt%). Further details on how the experiments were performed are included in the paper [Cardona *et al.* 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ces.2018.06.067).

# Annotations
These images were annotated with the particle locations using a combination of classical analysis (described in the Cardona paper above) and manual annotation (using a custom tool similar to [CVAT](https://www.cvat.ai/)). This set of annotations forms a ground truth to which results can be compared. Together, the images and ground truth form a *training dataset*, suitable for training a deep learning image instance segmentation/object detection model, such as the Mask R-CNN.

|Name|	Standard Polystyrene Microspheres|
| --- | --- |
|Problem type|	Object detection, Instance segmentation|
|Number of images|	2300 images with annotations 
|Microscopy type|	In-situ|
|Image format|	png|
|PAT hardware|	Mettler Toledo Particle Vision and Measurement (PVM v819)|

hypothesis: OpenCrystalData should be more ML-ready than Durham or Dryad, but likely more image-analysis-ready than event-learning-ready.
next_decision: Use OpenCrystalData as a comparison case for image-task-ready public data. Do not treat it as the main event-native benchmark unless internal file inspection reveals time/order/session structure. The optional concrete next step is to download the smallest 448 MB EasyViewer dataset and inspect whether its files can be reorganized into condition-indexed events.
preliminary_verdict: OpenCrystalData is much more programmatically inspectable than Dryad and is useful for image-analysis baselines. It preserves in-situ images, some process conditions, and auxiliary measurements. But the public metadata frames the datasets as image classification, segmentation, object-detection, anomaly-detection, or particle-size tasks. It does not expose an event manifest, time-ordered traces, failed/ambiguous attempts, or session/run-order provenance at the metadata level.
